question: What is the main goal of disaster preparedness in nursing?

options.A: To entirely prevent natural disasters from occurring in local communities
options.B: To reduce the financial operational costs of running a public hospital
options.C: To ensure a rapid and effective clinical response when a crisis strikes
options.D: To punish staff who fail to report for emergency duty shifts

explanation: You've got this! Preparedness is all about taking smart steps before a crisis hits so our healthcare teams can jump in quickly and save lives when emergencies happen. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why is planning ahead for disasters so crucial instead of just reacting when patients arrive?

options.A: Reacting on the spot is illegal under standard Nigerian healthcare labor laws
options.B: Casualties never arrive at a hospital unless an advanced warning schedule is posted
options.C: Pre-planning prevents the chaos and confusion that lead to preventable deaths during emergencies
options.D: Waiting for patients to arrive guarantees that medical supplies will never run out

explanation: Think of it like studying for exams early! Planning sets clear roles and routines, stopping a hectic situation from turning into a life-threatening disaster. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h1)

question: In disaster management, what exactly is a hazard?

options.A: The physical injury sustained by a patient during a sudden road traffic crash
options.B: The total financial loss suffered by a community after a major flood
options.C: A dangerous condition, substance, or activity that has the potential to cause harm
options.D: An official government document outlining hospital shift rosters during a strike

explanation: A hazard is the underlying threat itself (like a flooded river or loose electrical wire), while the actual disaster is the terrible event that happens when it strikes! [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the difference between vulnerability and capacity in a disaster setting?

options.A: Vulnerability is an administrative hospital term, while capacity is an emergency field nursing term
options.B: Vulnerability describes weaknesses that make people susceptible to harm, while capacity describes resources available to manage risk
options.C: Vulnerability refers exclusively to financial debt, while capacity refers strictly to building structures
options.D: Vulnerability is measured only after a disaster, while capacity is measured before any hazard appears

explanation: Vulnerability means what makes us prone to suffering (like weak buildings or lack of shelter), while capacity is our strength and resources to fight back! [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which health problem commonly happens right after severe flooding?

options.A: Immediate eradication of vector-borne parasites from local water tables
options.B: Outbreaks of waterborne illnesses like cholera and typhoid fever
options.C: A sudden spike in industrial chemical burn injuries across urban factories
options.D: Widespread occupational lung cancer among adult agricultural workers

explanation: When floodwaters mix with drinking sources, bacteria love it. That is why nurses always watch out for waterborne infections like cholera after floods! [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h3)

question: Following a sudden pipeline explosion, a hospital receives dozens of patients with severe burns. What immediate care will these patients need most?

options.A: A high demand for specialized fluid resuscitation, wound care, and pain management
options.B: A sudden requirement for widespread vector control and mosquito net distribution
options.C: An immediate influx of chronic malnutrition cases requiring outpatient nutritional counseling
options.D: A massive need for long-term physical therapy related to chronic stroke rehabilitation

explanation: Burn injuries cause massive fluid loss and intense pain. Nurses must act fast with IV fluids, careful wound dressings, and pain relief! [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the main focus of the 'preparedness' phase in disaster management?

options.A: Providing immediate search and rescue operations during an active earthquake
options.B: Conducting forensic investigations after a disaster has fully concluded
options.C: Rebuilding damaged roads and bridges months after floodwaters recede
options.D: Building operational readiness and planning before a disaster strikes

explanation: Preparedness always happens before the storm. It is all about running drills, stocking supplies, and getting your team ready so you are never caught off guard. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why do nurses practice regular emergency drills and simulations?

options.A: They turn theoretical plans into automatic, calm physical responses during chaotic crises
options.B: They replace the need for maintaining actual physical stock of emergency medications
options.C: They eliminate all forms of psychological stress for staff during real emergencies
options.D: They guarantee that hospitals will receive extra funding from international donors

explanation: Practice makes perfect! Regular drills mean that when a real emergency happens, your body and mind know what to do without freezing up. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h4)

question: What does a vulnerability assessment help a healthcare team figure out?

options.A: The personal home addresses of all senior hospital administrative staff
options.B: The exact daily profit margins of local pharmaceutical retail stores
options.C: Which nursing students achieved the highest grades in community health
options.D: Which populations and structures are most at risk during a local hazard

explanation: Spot-on! A vulnerability assessment helps us see who in the community is most likely to suffer, letting us protect them first. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h5)

question: A clinic is near a busy highway and a river that floods easily. Who should nurses prioritize first when planning an evacuation?

options.A: Elderly patients with mobility limitations and infants in the pediatric ward
options.B: Young administrative staff members who drive their own private cars to work
options.C: Healthy adult visitors waiting at the outpatient reception lobby
options.D: Off-duty nurses resting in the staff common room upstairs

explanation: Always save those who cannot help themselves first. Babies and immobile elders rely entirely on nurses to get them to safety! [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which management system do hospitals use during emergencies to keep a clear chain of command?

options.A: The Hospital Budget Allocation Matrix
options.B: The Nursing Process Evaluation Model
options.C: The Incident Command System (ICS)
options.D: The Primary Health Care Algorithm

explanation: In an emergency, everyone needs to know who is in charge. The ICS provides a clear, organized leadership structure so rescue efforts run smoothly. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h6)

question: Why do hospital disaster plans include steps for safely discharging stable patients?

options.A: To free up critical bed space and medical resources for incoming disaster casualties
options.B: To comply with international travel regulations for foreign medical volunteers
options.C: To punish patients who have overstayed their expected recovery duration
options.D: To reduce the hospital's monthly utility bills during a crisis event

explanation: When an emergency brings in dozens of critically injured people, sending home stable patients creates the vital bed space needed to save lives. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h6)

question: In mass casualty triage, what does a RED tag mean?

options.A: Minor cuts and bruises that can be treated with basic self-care methods
options.B: Immediate, life-threatening injuries requiring urgent intervention to save life
options.C: Stable injuries that can safely wait several hours for medical attention
options.D: Catastrophic injuries where the patient has little chance of survival

explanation: Red means 'Right now!' These patients have severe, life-threatening injuries and need our immediate care to survive. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h7)

question: During a building collapse, a nurse finds a victim who is unresponsive, not breathing even after opening the airway, and has no pulse. What triage tag should they get?

options.A: Green (Walking Wounded)
options.B: Red (Immediate)
options.C: Yellow (Delayed)
options.D: Black (Expectant / Deceased)

explanation: This is a tough call in mass casualty triage, but a black tag is used when injuries are so severe that resuscitation is impossible, allowing us to focus on survivors. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the main goal of Psychological First Aid (PFA) after a disaster?

options.A: To force survivors to recount every painful detail of their traumatic experience
options.B: To diagnose severe psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
options.C: To prescribe long-term antipsychotic medications to every disaster victim
options.D: To reduce initial emotional distress and support practical coping in survivors

explanation: PFA is about being a comforting, safe human presence. We help survivors feel grounded and secure without pushing them into therapy too soon. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h8)

question: Why should nurses avoid forcing disaster survivors to immediately talk about the graphic details of their trauma?

options.A: Survivors lose their legal right to medical treatment if they speak about the event
options.B: Hospital administrative policy strictly forbids nurses from listening to stories
options.C: Talking about trauma instantly causes permanent physical paralysis in adults
options.D: It can re-traumatize the individual and worsen acute psychological distress

explanation: Pushing someone to relive a horrific event before they are ready can overwhelm their mind and make their emotional shock even worse. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h8)

question: Which Nigerian government bodies coordinate national and state-level disaster management?

options.A: EFCC and ICPC
options.B: NEPA and PHCN
options.C: JAMB and WAEC
options.D: NEMA and SEMA

explanation: Good to know for your community health postings! NEMA handles things at the national level, while SEMA takes charge at the state level. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h9)

question: Why is working together across different agencies so vital during a major public health emergency?

options.A: External security forces take complete legal ownership of medical patient charts
options.B: Government regulations mandate that all agencies merge into a single permanent ministry
options.C: No single agency has enough resources or personnel to handle a major disaster alone
options.D: It eliminates the need for nurses to perform clinical triage duties in hospitals

explanation: Disasters are too big for just one group. By combining health workers, security, and transport agencies, everyone pitches in to save lives. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h9)

question: What is the main purpose of holding an after-action review (AAR) after responding to a disaster?

options.A: To assign criminal blame and penalize individual nurses for minor errors
options.B: To analyze successes and failures in order to improve future disaster plans
options.C: To permanently close down the hospital's emergency department services
options.D: To calculate exact profit margins generated by emergency room admissions

explanation: An after-action review is never about pointing fingers. It is a supportive team chat to see what went right and how we can do even better next time. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h10)

question: How do post-disaster debriefing sessions help nursing teams improve over time?

options.A: They allow staff to share real-world experiences and update protocols based on actual findings
options.B: They ensure that all medical equipment is automatically cleaned without human effort
options.C: They replace the need for conducting regular mock disaster simulations
options.D: They guarantee that future disasters will never happen in the local community

explanation: Listening to frontline nurses talk about what actually happened on the ground gives us the best feedback to upgrade our emergency guidelines! [learn more](GNS315_U1_T7#GNS315_U1_T7_h10)
